title: Hunting Hypothetical Particles in the Hair of Black Holes
hook: If ultralight bosons exist, a spinning black hole would grow a cloud of them and hum for years. LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA listened to two merger remnants, heard nothing, and ruled out a band of masses.
key_points: An ultralight boson around a spinning black hole would build up a cloud that radiates long-lived gravitational waves.
The collaboration ran directed searches for such long-transient signals from two recent merger remnants.
No signal was found in either target, from GW250114 or GW250207.
That disfavours vector boson masses of roughly 2.8 to 4.0 x 10^-13 eV at over 90% confidence.
A second, independent constraint comes from black holes that are still spinning fast — a cloud would have slowed them.
The spin-based limits depend on assumed black hole age, so the excluded ranges are quoted for a 10^5-year benchmark.
content_html: Plenty of theories predict "ultralight bosons" — particles so light they're far below anything a collider could make, but a natural dark matter candidate. Remarkably, black holes can hunt them. If such a particle exists, it accumulates around a rapidly spinning black hole into a cloud, feeding off the hole's rotation; the cloud then radiates gravitational waves for a long time afterwards. So a black hole is, in effect, a particle detector you don't have to build.
extra_html: The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration has now applied this to data from the second and third parts of the fourth observing run. They ran directed searches, using a hidden-Markov-model tracking scheme, for long-transient waves from vector boson clouds around the remnants of the mergers that produced GW250114 and GW250207. Neither target showed anything. At a threshold corresponding to a 1% false alarm probability, that disfavours vector boson masses in the range 2.80 to 3.95 × 10⁻¹³ eV with greater than 90% confidence. They also apply a second and rather elegant argument: growing a cloud costs the black hole its spin, so a black hole observed still spinning fast can't have had one. From the inferred high spins in three binaries (GW240515, GW241113, GW241225_08), they exclude further ranges of scalar and vector boson masses — though those limits depend on how long the black hole has existed, which is why the numbers are quoted at a benchmark age of 10⁵ years.

flashcards.prompt: How could a spinning black hole reveal an ultralight boson?
flashcards.back_html: The boson would accumulate into a cloud around the hole, which then radiates long-lived gravitational waves — a persistent hum rather than a merger's brief chirp.

flashcards.prompt: How does a black hole's *spin* alone constrain these particles, with no signal detected?

choices.text: Growing a boson cloud drains the hole's spin, so black holes still spinning fast rule out bosons in the relevant mass range
Fast spin makes the black hole emit the bosons directly as radiation
Spin changes the black hole's mass enough to be measured

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors derive limits from the inferred high spins of constituent black holes in three binaries — a cloud would have spun them down, so high spin excludes those boson masses.

flashcards.prompt: Why are the spin-based exclusion ranges quoted with an assumed black hole age?

choices.text: The cloud takes time to grow and drain spin, so how long the hole has existed sets which masses it could have shed
Older black holes are harder to detect with LIGO
The particle's mass changes as the universe expands

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper quotes limits at 10^5 years, matching typical dynamically formed binaries, precisely because the excluded mass range depends on the assumed age.
